name: Copper Red
lede: Copper red is a reddish orange named for an object, the kind of name early nineteenth-century naturalists used in their color lists and later dropped.

sections.title: A name from the object
sections.body:
Copper red belongs to the family of color names that point at a thing rather than a hue: grass green, lead grey, copper red. It turns up again and again in the early nineteenth-century lists that grew out of Werner's mineralogical color scheme, which Baty traces in a chart of lists from the 1790s to the 1810s [1]. The lists differ, and copper red shuffles between neighbors such as scarlet red, blood red and carmine red from one list to the next [1].

That shuffling is a clue. The name was never pinned to one chip, and our sources do not say which shade of copper was meant: the metal, its tarnish or the red mineral that forms on its ore [1]. Who first used the phrase as a color is undocumented in the books we have.

sections.title: Dropped from the final list
sections.body:
When Patrick Syme published his illustrated edition of Werner's *Nomenclature of Colours* in 1821, it ran to 110 numbered colors [2]. The reds in that list include tile red, [[scarlet]] red (no. 84), vermilion red (no. 85), aurora red (no. 86), arterial blood red (no. 87) and flesh red (no. 88), but not copper red [2]. The name stayed in the older lists, yet it did not make the edition that circulated in scientific and medical circles.

The reason for the omission is not recorded, but a contemporary complaint is suggestive. The optician James Hunter noted in 1841 that a color named for an object only works for people who already know that object at first hand, and he gave copper red as one of his examples [3]. Without a printed swatch the name conveys little.

sections.title: Two copper reds in the paint box
sections.body:
In the pigment trade the phrase meant a material. A catalogue by Salter from 1869 lists two copper reds: copper oxide, which is the mineral cuprite, and an organic copper compound said to come from a bird called the turaco [4]. Salter relays Professor Church's report of a copper-bearing pigment in the feathers of the violet plantain-eater and two other turaco species, which Church named turacine and which was, by this account, the first animal or vegetable pigment found with copper as an essential element [5].

Cuprite itself is red copper(I) oxide, Cu2O, a common mineral of the weathered zones of copper ore deposits, with Cornwall and Clifton, Arizona among the places named [6]. A basic copper chromate, meanwhile, is reported in the literature in a range of colors from yellow to chocolate brown, with copper red among them [7].

sections.title: Which red is the swatch
sections.body:
The swatch on this page, #CB6D51, was filed from four sources: Wikipedia, ISCC-NBS 1955, Maerz and Paul 1930 and Werner [8]. The ISCC-NBS system calls it a moderate reddish orange, a match within 0.6 units, and the nearest everyday name is [[terracotta]] [8]. The library merges it with Werner's aurora red as a near duplicate, 2.0 units away, and the Werner example objects attached to it (the vent feathers of a woodpecker, the red on a naked apple, red orpiment) belong to Werner's no. 86 [8][2].

So the chip is a terracotta-like orange-red, closer to [[brick-red]] or fired clay than to a polished penny. Treat it as a screen color, not a recipe.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 176 works, about 0.7 per cent [9]. India dominates: 75 of its 721 paintings carry it, 14 times the archive rate [9]. The Kalighat, Rajput and Pahari schools reach 17 of 96, 15 of 97 and 14 of 118, and no Impressionist work among 140 does [9].

The earliest match is a four-armed Maitreya of about 1150, and the largest is Émile Bernard's *[[painting:commons-Q17490794|Symbolic Self-Portrait]]* of 1891, where it covers 60 per cent of the canvas [9]. It is a middle tone, not a shadow or highlight, in 55 per cent of the places it appears [9]. Its closest company in the archive is [[vermilion]] and [[terracotta]] [9]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so read them as screen colors [9].

questions.q: Why did the optician James Hunter criticize color names like copper red in 1841?
choices: They only convey a color to people who already know the object
They were too long to print
They named colors nobody could paint
They came from a foreign language
questions.answer: They only convey a color to people who already know the object

questions.q: Copper red is one of the 110 numbered colors in Syme's 1821 edition.
Which mineral did Salter's 1869 list name as one of the two copper reds?

openers: Copper red appears in many early color lists, yet not in the 110 colors of Syme's 1821 standard.
In 1869 one catalogue listed two copper reds: a mineral and a pigment from the feathers of an African bird.
Look for this orange-red in Indian miniatures: 75 of 721 in our archive carry it, 14 times the archive rate.

issues: Removed unsourced list-length range (70 to just over 100).
Removed unsourced 'everyday speech' survival claim; softened 'standard most naturalists used' to circulation in scientific and medical circles.
